profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a consumer lending fintech about a six-week pilot of a new collections decision engine for early-stage delinquent accounts. The engine uses a risk-sensitive sequential decision policy that weighs immediate repayment actions against longer-run downside such as roll rates, complaints, and hardship outcomes. The agenda is to confirm what the September pilot includes, what will be compared against the baseline, what each team must deliver, how weekly performance will be reviewed, and whether the team is on track to be ready by September 15. The expected outcome is an agreed pilot plan with owners, dependencies, and a timeline that both participants believe is aligned.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: Collections operations, digital treatment design, pilot launches, cross-functional rollout planning
members.background: Elena came up through operations strategy at two fintech lenders and now owns product delivery for delinquency treatment programs across app, SMS, and email channels.
members.private_state: She needs this pilot to start on time because leadership wants visible Q3 progress, and she is trying to avoid a repeat of a prior analytics project that was technically complete but not operationally launchable.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'baseline,' they mean the current live U.S. digital collections waterfall that operations is using today for the target segment.
A 'pilot-ready package' includes not just the decision logic but also the monitoring deck, agent guidance, compliance-facing summary, and launch checklist needed for live traffic.
A 'weekly readout' should use Monday-through-Sunday operating weeks with near-realized repayment and complaint indicators so the business can steer the pilot in real time.
Being 'ready by September 15' means customer traffic starts that day with all business-facing materials already in place.

members.name: David Romero
members.expertise: Sequential decision models, risk-sensitive optimization, policy evaluation, production scoring design
members.background: David leads the decision science team building treatment policies for lending lifecycle interventions and has recently adapted a recursive risk framework into the collections policy stack.
members.private_state: He wants to preserve methodological credibility and avoid premature business interpretation of noisy early results, while keeping his team focused on policy design rather than operational collateral.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the 'baseline,' they mean the incumbent champion policy used in the last analytics evaluation, including the broader digital delinquency cohort used in model comparison.
A 'pilot-ready policy' means the action table, parameter settings, and API configuration are finalized and handed off; dashboards, training, and business collateral are separate workstreams.
A 'weekly readout' should be built from action-date cohorts with at least a 14-day observation window so comparisons are not distorted by immature outcomes.
Being 'ready by September 15' means the model is frozen and delivered in time for engineering deployment during that release cycle, not necessarily that live customer exposure begins that morning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the baseline' when discussing expected pilot comparisons.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the current production rules used by collections operations for the live U.S. digital segment targeted for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the incumbent champion policy from the most recent model evaluation dataset, which spans a somewhat broader digital delinquency population.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this organization, 'baseline' is standard shorthand and each person hears it as the obvious reference from their own workflow, so the phrase feels precise enough even though they are anchoring on different artifacts.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a pilot-ready package
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the team needs a 'pilot-ready policy/package' by the target date.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the policy logic plus launch dashboards, operations guidance, and compliance-facing documentation needed to run the pilot end to end.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only the policy output itself: action tables, thresholds, configuration, and the handoff documentation required for engineering integration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants are cooperative and routinely use 'policy' as a compact term; each silently bundles the adjacent work their own function normally treats as inherent, so neither hears a mismatch.

misalignment_points.topic: What the first weekly readout will look like
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have a 'weekly readout' once the pilot starts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a Monday-through-Sunday business review showing booked cash, contact outcomes, and early complaint signals for the prior operating week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a report based on action-date cohorts that are held until they have about 14 days of outcome development, even if that shifts the apparent reporting week.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A weekly readout sounds like a routine reporting detail, so neither person thinks to unpack the cohorting logic, and both assume the other is using the default convention from their own team.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both commit to being 'ready by September 15' for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats this as the date when live customer traffic begins under the new policy, with operational dependencies already completed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats this as the date by which the policy is finalized and transferred for deployment in the September release process, with production traffic potentially starting later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Date commitments often sound fully aligned at the surface, and both meanings are common in cross-functional planning, so the phrase creates false consensus without triggering clarification.
